q.intro.text: A forty-eight dollar jacket is twenty-five percent off. Mia finds the discount as one fourth of forty-eight dollars. Leo works out zero point two five times forty-eight. Who is right? Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the picture moves first, then the notation.

e.step0.text: Twenty-five percent means twenty-five hundredths. That is one fourth, and it is zero point two five. Three names, one point on the line.

e.step1.text: The fraction route: one fourth of forty-eight dollars. Cut the bar into four equal parts: one part is twelve dollars. One easy division, forty-eight divided by four.

e.step2.text: The decimal route: zero point two five times forty-eight. Twenty-five times forty-eight is twelve hundred, and two decimal places make twelve. Same point, same twelve dollars.

e.step3.text: Both routes are right. Forty-eight splits evenly into four, so the fraction is quicker in your head. Report it as money: a twelve dollar discount.

e.why.text: Quick check: why do both routes give twelve dollars?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. The same number times the same forty-eight gives the same answer, every time.

e.why.differ.text: It is never luck. Two correct routes for the same number always agree.

e.why.one.text: Both routes are real. Any route that keeps the number the same is valid: pick the shorter one.

t.intro.text: Now you leave an eighteen percent tip on a forty-five dollar bill. The first step is done for you.

t.route.text: Eighteen percent is eighteen hundredths, or zero point one eight. No friendly fraction this time. Which route suits these numbers?

t.route.ok.text: Yes: ten percent is easy to find, and eight percent is eight pieces of one percent. Then add.

t.route.div.text: Eighteen percent is not one eighteenth. That gives two dollars fifty, a tiny tip.

t.route.times.text: Eighteen percent is zero point one eight, not eighteen. That gives eight hundred ten dollars, a tip bigger than the bill!

t.ten.text: Find ten percent of forty-five dollars.

t.ten.ok.text: Yes: ten percent of forty-five dollars is four dollars fifty, one tenth of the bar.

t.ten.point.text: The point is one place off. Ten percent is one tenth: forty-five dollars divided by ten.

t.ten.no.text: Ten percent is one tenth: split forty-five dollars into ten equal parts.

t.total.text: Eight percent is eight times forty-five cents, three dollars sixty. So what is the whole eighteen percent tip?

t.total.ok.text: Yes: four fifty plus three sixty is eight dollars ten. Same answer as zero point one eight times forty-five, with no long multiplication.

t.total.part.text: Three sixty is only the eight percent part. Add the ten percent part too.

t.total.no.text: Eighteen percent is ten percent plus eight percent: add four fifty and three sixty.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked both, and you were right: one number, so every correct route gives the same answer.

q.cb.one.text: At the start you picked only Leo. Mia’s fraction route was just as right, and here a third route, ten percent plus eight percent, was the quickest.

q.cb.differ.text: At the start you thought the amounts could differ. They can’t: one number gives one answer. You just pick the route that suits the numbers.

q.cb.none.text: One number, three names: pick the form that makes the numbers easy, then report the answer in the form the context needs.

p.intro.text: Three cousins share a nine hundred dollar prize. Ava gives each cousin thirty-three percent: zero point three three times nine hundred is two hundred ninety-seven dollars. She says that is exactly one third of the prize. Is Ava right?

p.test.text: Let’s test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Right. One third is zero point three three three, and the threes never stop. Zero point three three is a rounded third.

p.c2.text: Right. Cut the bar into three equal parts: each is exactly three hundred dollars.

p.c3.text: Right. Zoom in on the end of the bar: Ava’s three shares stop at eight hundred ninety-one dollars, so nine dollars is left out.

p.no.inexact.text: Some decimals are exact: zero point two five is exactly one fourth. The trouble is that one third never stops.

p.no.mid.text: It can: a tiny gap times nine hundred is three dollars per cousin.

p.no.calc.text: A screen cuts digits off. One third is zero point three three three, forever.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That’s a proof. Ava rounded first, so her shares miss nine dollars. Here the fraction one third is exact, and easier: nine hundred divided by three.
